title: Victor Haghani – The Last of the Tactical Allocators (S7E13)

My guest today is Victor Hagani, founder of Elmwelf.

That might be because Victor wouldn't categorize himself as such.
Rather he sees his dynamic index investing approach not as a tactical alternative to traditional
static portfolios, but rather as the rational approach for anyone starting from first principles.
This conversation dances between theory and implementation.
Victor is just as comfortable sharing his thoughts on where equity market risk comes

If you're passionate about asset allocation, you'll find lots to think about in this
one.
Please enjoy my conversation with Victor Hagani.
Victor welcome to the podcast, excited to have you here, I actually started reading all

I think it is some of the most lucid, clear writing on thinking about investing and even

So really appreciate everything you put out in the space and very excited to chat today.
Thank you for joining me.
Thanks Corey.
It's great to be on the podcast.
I love your podcast.
I've enjoyed many different sessions you've had with your guests.
Thank you so much.
David, you started your career in the 1980s, famously or infamously attached to long-term
capital management of which there has been so much ink spilled.
You've spoken about so much.
I want to start after that.
Listeners, if you want to get Victor's take on that stuff, this isn't the episode.
We want to start in 2011, some three decades after you started your career, some 15 years
or so after long-term capital management, take me to that time.
What inspired you to launch Elm?
What type of problem were you trying to ultimately solve?
So we have to go back a few years before 2011, but 2011 is when I founded our wealth management
firm Elm Wealth.
But after LTCM, I woke up and it wasn't a dream.
And I realized that I needed to focus on managing my family's savings and up until that time
I had worked at an investment bank that took a lot of my compensation and put it into
the stock of the company Solomon and then at LTCM, it was pretty natural to invest a lot
of my savings in our fund that we managed.
Here it was, you know, around 2000, 2001, and I was like, geez, I've got to really figure
out how to invest for my family.
And it was kind of a shocking realization to see that I'd been working in finance already
for like 17 years, working with some really brilliant minds, practitioners and academics.
And yet I had never really thought much about investing for myself.
All of my focus was on research to begin with and then proprietary trading.
And my situation was really typical, too.
You come out of college, you go to Wall Street and you get trained in everything to do with
Wall Street, unless you're going into a private wealth area, which Solomon didn't even
have at the time, you don't really get trained at all in terms of what to do with personal
finance.
So there I was.
And the natural thing to do is I kind of looked around and saw what my friends and people
I respected were doing and everybody was following this concept of the Yale endowment model
that David Swenson was making so popular and Yale's returns were making so attractive.
There I was, you know, I kind of knew a bunch of people in private equity, the hedge fund
space venture distress and I just started to invest as if as though I were the Yale endowment
or something.
One man, Yale endowment.
And meanwhile I was taking a sabbatical from working, my kids were young and I wanted
to spend time with them.
And eventually maybe I don't know exactly when after four or five years, I just kind of
had this realization that what I was doing just made no sense at all.
It made no sense from a life point of view.
It made no sense from a risk and fee-paying point of view.
The straw that broke the camel's back on that approach to investing was when I sat down
with my accountant, David, untracked and went over my tax return for one of those years.
And I was like, but David, why am I paying all this tax?
I haven't had that much income this year and he was like, well, you have this income
here is short-term capital gains and you have these expenses here that you can't deduct
from your income because it's these miscellaneous itemized deductions.
And it was like this epiphany of, geez, what am I doing?
I've got to go back to basics.
I've got to invest in index funds.
I started to move the ship towards indexing and immediately a bunch of questions came up.
Okay, well, I'm going to invest in index funds.
How much should I put in stocks versus bonds?
How much should I have in non-US equities versus US equities?
How do I think about these different things?
They weren't such difficult questions, but they were questions that needed answers.
And as I thought about these things, I was kind of informed by experiences that I had
had up until then, which some of the seminal experiences and thinking about equities for
me was being in Japan in the late eighties working for Solomon Brothers and just being there
in the middle of this crazy run-up in valuations and Japanese equities were trading at PEs
of 100 for the whole broad market.
And yet people were saying, no way is they're going to keep going higher.
And I think that Japanese equities represented close to 50 percent of global market caps.
So I kind of felt like I wanted to have some guardrails and some monitoring of my index
investing.
I didn't want to just say, boom, I'm just going to be totally passive market cap indexing
and that's it.
And never change anything and just take the market caps because I kind of felt like sometimes
it really pays to have your eyes open and be thinking about long-term returns.
Not only was this whole late eighties in Japan, but then like another decade or more
later, I'm sitting there and just seeing this whole internet bubble going on in 99, 2000.
And again, now I'm in 2006 and I'm looking back on that and saying, geez, again, I love
the idea of indexing low cost, diversification, tax efficiency.
But if I'm sitting in 2000, 2001, I want to be kind of responding to that.
I mean, that was a time when tips were yielding 4% long-term US tips and US and non-US equity
markets were trading at PEs of 25 or higher or earnings yields of 4% or lower.
And I would have wanted to not have that many equities back then.
These ideas really informed how I wanted to invest in index funds.
So eventually a name for this approach to investing came my way, dynamic index investing.
And then as I was talking to friends and former colleagues, et cetera, about what I was
doing with my wealth, people started to show interest and say, well, if you did that
really professionally and properly, we'd like you to manage some of our money.
And so the idea to set up Elm wealth was born.
There was nobody offering anything like it.
And I thought the things that we could control fees, taxes, diversification were all this
low-hanging fruit that I needed to pick and to share.
So we set up the firm in 2011.
I set fees at 12 basis points per year as the only fee, which I thought was appropriate.
If you're going to invest in index funds, you shouldn't charge a high fee for helping
people to do that.
And the asset allocation that we were coming up with was based on publicly available research
that lots of people had done and just felt like, okay, full transparency, low fees, tax
efficiency, let's go.
And that became the start of Elm in 2011.
I think of the timeline here.
A lot of people take for granted today the proliferation of exchange traded funds.
But 2011 was still early days.
The first funds were launched in the early 90s, depending on which historian you talked
to.
But it was really post-2008 that ETFs exploded in popularity.
How much of what you're able to do today is actually predicated on the emergence of ETFs?
What we do today, we could not have done 20 years ago.
So first of all, 20 years ago, the only really low-cost index funds in ETFs were primarily
for US equities.
I mean, there were some international equity index funds that Vanguard had, but they were
still fairly expensive.
And lots of other asset classes, there were not low-cost index funds.
I remember back in the 90s wanting to get some high yield exposure and there were no
high yield index funds at all.
There were no muni index funds at all back then, if I recall.
So that's one aspect of it.
But the other aspect is just the transactions costs, custody fees, all of that were so
high 15 years ago.
If you wanted to do a separately managed account at Fidelity, the commissions on doing trades
could be as much as $25 a trade, then by the time we got started, doing separately managed
to count said L, commissions on ETFs were down to $5 a trade and then eventually went
to zero after Robinhood turned up.
The technology, the outsourcing, everything has come together to make what we do today
possible, but it wasn't possible to do it 15 years ago.
So before we dive into the details, I want to start sort of at a 30,000 foot view of
the strategy that you have ended up implementing today at Elm, this dynamic asset allocation process.
Can you talk a little bit about the philosophies behind the process without getting into those
nitty gritty details and how those philosophies end up translating into maybe a top level
portfolio view of what you're trying to accomplish?
The best way to describe what we do is imagine that we live in a world which the academics
love to use this world.
We live in a world where there's one risky asset, call it the global equity market or the
global market portfolio of risky assets and there's one safe asset, call it tips or call
it whatever you want, treasury bills, some safe asset and you're trying to decide how
much of your savings you want to put in the risky asset.
That's the only choice you have.
You have a choice of the safe asset or the risky asset and you want to decide how much
should I put in there?
The amount that you should put in there has to be a function of three things.
It has to be a function of how attractive it is.
What is the expected return of this risky asset relative to the safe asset?
It has to be a function of how risky is the risky asset relative to the safe asset and
it has to be a function of your personal degree of risk aversion.
There's no other way to make that decision or no other way that I can think of to make
that decision that's at all rational or sensible.
Risk aversion is something that locally should stay pretty constant over time.
There's not reasons why our personal preference is with regard to risk aversion arises from
the decreasing marginal utility of wealth and it should be relatively stable through time
and over some range of wealth levels.
What it comes down to is that your asset allocation, how much you allocate to the risky asset,
it should be a function of expected return relative to the safe asset of the risky asset
and the risky asset's risk.
That's what we do.
We just say, okay, we have clients and we say to the client, let's try to figure out
your degree of risk aversion and we'll talk about that in a bit.
Once we have that, we say, okay, we're going to come up with an estimate of the long-term
expected return of equities relative to the safe asset.
This is something that every large investment firm has their expectations for returns
of equities and you can just look it up online or you could go to our website, we publish
our capital market assumptions too, but Vanguard, BlackRock, Morgan Stanley, everybody has
their capital market assumptions and to a large extent, they're bunched together for long-term
return expectations.
The riskiness of the market, there's lots of ways of looking at that.
We can tell when we're in early 2020, it was pretty risky and uncertain.
Other times, the market is very docile and peaceful and it's really easy to observe
that. That should drive your asset allocation.
Really can't see what's a really good rational alternative to that.
I think that there's other things that you can do if you don't have the time or the inclination
or the ability to incorporate expected returns and risk into your asset allocation, but
I don't know of a sounder approach to investing than that.
You mentioned these three critical elements you have to measure, one of which is going
to be very client-centric.
I know from our prior discussions that you have a set of onboarding questions, you need
to ask clients before you can calibrate this dynamic process to their wants and needs.
Let's start with those onboarding questions.
What are you asking clients and why do you see this as such an important part of your process?
The first question that we ask clients is we say to them, we're going to manage some
of your savings.
Please tell us how much of your account you would like to have invested in equities in
a hypothetical world in which we agree that equities have an expected return of 4 percent
above the safe asset return and that equity risk is kind of in the middle.
We're not at a very elevated level.
We're not at a very quiet level of equity, market, volatility, and uncertainty.
Tell us how much equities you want in your account in that hypothetical world.
That's setting a baseline exposure to equities in this 4 percent expected return world.
That's the most important question that we ask them.
In some sense, that's really asking two questions bunched into one in that case.
We're asking them a question of what's their risk aversion and we're also asking them,
what do they think is normal equity market risk?
We're combining those two things together because we could try to calibrate their risk
aversion separately, but then we'd have to really make them think about what risk level
do we mean and do they mean by normal equity market risk?
When people answer that question, are clients really bunched together?
We have over 400 clients, individuals and families, and people answer that question.
They say, you know, I'd like to have between 50 and 100 percent in equities in that case.
Each client has a different number, but in general, clients kind of think that 4 percent
expected returns normal equity risk.
Yeah, I'd like to have 75 percent in equities in that case or some other client is maybe
younger or more risk tolerant since I want to have 100 percent.
Somebody else is like, I want to have 55 percent.
We don't get too many people that want less than 50 percent.
We sort of tie it back to some classical finance formulas like the Merton share, but kind of
all ties out really nicely to a level of risk aversion that we think typifies most
thoughtful investors out there.
We've also tried to calibrate risk aversion directly by asking people questions about
gambles, such as imagine that you're flipping a coin and you're going to bet some of your
wealth on it.
It's a fair coin.
If it comes up tails, you're going to lose 20 percent of your wealth and if it comes
up heads, you're going to increase your wealth by 35 percent.
How do you feel about that?
Is that something you really like?
Is that something you don't like?
Is that something you're indifferent to?
We can ask a bunch of questions like that to also calibrate risk aversion.
We did a survey like that and wrote about it a few years ago.
We found that from over 100 people that took that survey, people really bunched together.
I'm sure a lot of your listeners are familiar with the Kelly Criterion, which is like a good
way of thinking about risk aversion.
What we found was that this broad range of over 100 investors had risk aversion that
would be two to three times as risk aversion that a Kelly better or a Kelly investor would
have.
Let's get into the portfolio construction process itself.
Calibrate to an investor's preferences and then you need to start running this weekly
dynamic process.
You talked a little bit about needing expected returns and risk measures.
How are you actually capturing those expected returns and risk measures?
How are those inputs that you're capturing, translating into target weights?
There's a lot of consensus on what is the long-term expected return of a big broad stock
market, the US market or all non-US equity markets, even the global market for that matter.
The strongest consensus among market observers and researchers is that the earnings yield,
the cyclically adjusted earnings yield of a broad stock market, is a decent, simple
and one of the best estimates of the long-term expected real return of that equity market.
The cyclically adjusted earnings yield, what we mean is take the last 10 years of earnings
adjusted for inflation, average it together and divided by today's index price, the price
of the stock market, and that's your earnings yield.
It makes some sense.
There's assumptions that are built into that.
The assumption that's the way to think about it is that all of these companies are like
a big machine and they're producing earnings from this big machine and the earnings are
coming out.
If the companies paid out all of their earnings as dividends, that these machines would still
be able to produce the same amount of profit year after year adjusted for inflation.
That's a really simple and turns out empirically a reasonable model for how
corporate earnings work.
In practice, especially in the US these days, companies don't pay out all of their earnings
as dividends.
They never really have even going back a century but payout ratio is used to be higher.
Since companies retain some of their earnings, you expect their earnings to grow a little
faster because they're investing some of the retained earnings or they're investing all
of the retained earnings and trying to increase capacity.
That modeling of earnings is both simple.
It's reasonable and it is not refuted by history.
I wouldn't say that we look at history and it says, yeah, this is what things look like
and so we say, great, but here's this model and we look at it historically and it actually
fits history pretty well also.
That's the expected long-term real return of equities.
This adjustment for retained earnings is something that we do at Elm.
We've written about it, Schiller and Campbell that gave us the Campbell Schiller Cape number.
They wanted to keep things really simple and they wanted to use Cape more as a regression
variable rather than using earnings yield as just a pure straight up predictor of long-term
expected returns.
We make this adjustment for payout ratios and that bumps up earnings yield a little bit
for all the different markets and so that's what we use.
We're using that as a predictor of the long-term real arithmetic return, the average annual
return, not the compound return.
When we compare it to what other people are forecasting, like if we go to Vanguard's website
and type in Vanguard capital market assumptions and see that they're giving a number for
US equities over the next 10 years of say 4.5%.
Our number is number one, it's nominal.
Our expected return is a real number so we have to make an adjustment for inflation to
see how close we are to each other and then our number is arithmetic and there's a geometric,
so we need to make an adjustment for a 10-year geometric compound return versus a 10-year
arithmetic return.
When we do that, we actually find that if you look at 4 or 5 of these places, Vanguard,
BlackRock, etc., and maybe you throw out GMO who thinks US equities are going to have
a negative return because they have a mean reversion and a multiple built-in.
You throw out highs and lows and go with the people in the middle, you'll notice that
at least today, the average is more or less centered on this earnings yield number for
the broad market.
That's our long-term expected real return for equities so we have to compare it to a long-term
real return for a safe asset and the long-term real return for a safe asset, the best place
to look is the yield on tips.
We subtract one from the other and that gives us what we could call the risk premium and
we're going to compare that to 4%, which is our baseline number that I was talking about
earlier, and we're going to overweight or underweight the equity market or the equity exposure
for our client proportionally to that, which again is the simple and sensible way to do
that.
That's the thing that's kind of stable over time.
It doesn't move around that much.
It does move around, but it doesn't move around that much that quickly.
The riskiness of the market is more volatile.
Risk is more volatile than return, as we know, especially short-term risk.
For risk, we could have, and we thought about it at the time, just look at risk directly,
look at the VIX index, look at short-term options, or slightly longer-term equity options, and
look at the implied volatility or do some blend between implied volatility and realize
the historic volatility.
We thought that there were some challenges in doing that.
I think we could have done that.
That would have been a reasonable thing to do.
Instead, we decided to use another metric, which is collinear with volatility.
We decided to use a momentum metric.
Comparing today's index level to a one-year moving average, adjusted for inflation and risk
premium or total return and risk premium, using momentum is like a good stand-in proxy
for measuring risk more directly.
It has some benefits.
It's super simple.
You can set it up so like half the time you're in a more risky state, and half the time
it's positive, half the time it's negative on average, with choosing to use risk directly.
We would have to come up with, what do we think is the centering point for that?
Also, if we were using risk directly, we'd really have a lot of turnover because using

We would be generating a lot of turnover if we were tracking that.
We would wind up doing some post-processing on it, and by that time, now we have a measure
that our investors would be like, okay, this kind of feels a little black boxy to me.
We thought momentum is nice and solid.
It's coincident with the direct risk measure.
If you go back historically and look at times when momentum is positive, market volatility
is more subdued and vice versa.
We use momentum as a proxy for risk.
When momentum is positive, we deem that a low risk environment.
We increase exposures by a third basically to the equity market, and vice versa, when
momentum is negative, that tends to be a higher risk environment where we decrease client
exposure to equities.
That's how we're doing it, and we're looking at every client's portfolio, every client's
account on a weekly basis, and we're moving them towards these targets that we have that
come from those metrics.
It's all very transparent.
People can see the asset allocation, targets on the website.
We have to manage everybody's account, especially taxable accounts, taking into consideration tax
effects from the rebalancing that we're doing.
We don't want to have too much turnover in people's accounts, people don't like that, and
we don't like that.
We're targeting people to a four week moving average.
There's other little implementation details, but it's all fully transparent in terms
of how we do it.
I want to push in on some of these metrics a little bit, and get your detailed thoughts,
because there are critiques to things like Kate, Bersickically Adjusted Arning's yield,
particularly when you're talking, they're measuring it on a time series basis, or looking
at it cross sectionally, across different regions.
There's arguments that it doesn't really adequately account for things like differences
in industry composition, or changes in profit margins over time.
How would you address these critiques in your use of Kate, Bersickically Adjusted Arning's
yield?
The first thing I would say is that simplicity is a merit, and so I think the benefit of
simplicity has to be weighed against, perhaps a better estimate with a more complex estimate
that takes more things into account, and trying to find that balance is important.
With complexity, you're always going to have to guard against a backfit bias.
You have to realize you're never going to get the expected return.
You're always going to get something's higher or lower than that.
You don't want to get into a raise to the bottom in terms of just fitting what we've just
seen behind us.
Now, in terms of those specific critiques, a lot of people say, look, US equities are trading
at twice the multiple, or half the earnings yield of the rest of the world, but that's just
because the US has so much tech and the rest of the world doesn't.
Well, actually, you could really do that analysis.
We've done it.
We've published about it.
It's really straightforward, and if you would make the whole world have the same industry
composition, so take the whole world's industry composition average, and now, say, imagine
that the US has the same industry composition as the whole world, and the non-US market also
has the same industry composition as the whole world.
That makes a small difference to earnings yield in PE, but not much.
If the earnings yield of US equities is just over 3%, and the rest of the world is just
over 6%, so call it a 3% difference, this industry composition represents about 50 basis points
of that.
So, about one-sixth of the difference.
I can't speak that much about profit margins, but obviously, business has changed over time.
First of all, accounting metrics change over time, so when we're looking at how gap
accounting worked in the 1960s or 1980s, or today, or how accounting metrics are going
to be reported 20 years from now, they're definitely moving.
But again, from a simplicity point of view, we think they haven't moved all that much,

And so, there's a ton of things that you can criticize about how earnings are calculated

At the end of the day, when we think about this balance between simplicity and not making
our metrics be return-chasing metrics, we just have said we'd rather just keep something
simple and stable through time rather than making a lot of modifications to it.
A lot of the criticisms are fair, but I think that at the same time, the sickly adjusted earnings
yield is the single best metric that is out there.
People are saying, oh, you know what I'm going to do is I'm going to use forecasted earnings
and combine that with historical earnings, and that will be like a blended number.
That's good.
I mean, you have a problem there that it's a little bit harder to use that historically because
we didn't have good earnings forecast going further back, but I think that's a reasonable
thing to do.
When you do that, it doesn't change things that much.
Overall, I think earnings yields points in the right direction.
I mean, I just think that whatever adjustments you make, I just don't think you can say
that US equities have a 6% earnings yield.
I just don't think there's any way of coming up with US equities has a 6% long-term return
above inflation when the earnings yield is at 3%.
I don't think it's that wrong.
Whatever you do, it's going to be around 3%, and a lot of people have published stuff
about that like, what would we need for US equities to return 10% over the next 10 years?
The only reasonable way to get that would be multiple expansion.
I mean, it's just not that reasonable.
Historically, we've had all of these massive revolutions in technology productivity, et cetera.
We just never see earnings do what they would need to do to justify, to be consistent
with today's earnings yields indicating 8% real returns for US equities.
You mentioned using tips as the basis for measuring real returns, and two questions
come up there.
I'm sure there'll be listeners who would critique the idea of using CPI as a measure of inflation,
so that's one side of it.
But the other that comes to mind for me is someone who's run dynamic processes like this
is tips tend to have a liquidity issue in a crisis, and so I could see that you could
end up with potentially very highly skewed or incorrect measures of your inflation-adjusted
earnings yield precisely in those periods where you would expect the portfolio to be the
most dynamic.
How do you think about those problems?
First of all, let's agree that if you're going to use earnings yield, that earnings yield
is an estimate of the long-term real return of equities, so we have to compare it against
the real return of a safe asset.
If we think that the yield on tips is wrong at some point in some sense, I think that's
what you're saying, that they could be trading at 3%, but that's a bad signal.
They're really a 2%.
Well, the thing is that you can buy tips.
If I wake up one day and US equities has an earnings yield of 3%, and I can buy 30
your tips at 4%, and I say, you know what?
These tips, all these relative value players had to sell them.
They should really be at 2%, but somehow they're at 4%, well, I don't care.
I'm just going to buy them.
They're relevant, even though I do agree that they tend to trade cheap.
I think that they are a real thing that you can buy from that point of view, even to
the extent that they suffer from maybe not being the best estimates of the real return.
They're a tradable estimate of the real return, and so I think that means that makes sense.
In terms of CPI, again, we're just trying to compare like for like, we're thinking about
a return estimate for US equities as thinking about it relative to CPI.
So we just want to measure apples to apples when we're thinking about risk premium.
So even if CPI is not a great measure, like if CPI is maybe under-representing inflation,
we're getting that on both sides of the comparison, if we think about equity returns relative
to CPI as well.
When we talk about market risk, there are maybe three big drivers that tend to come up.
Riches in discount rates, changes in earning expectations, and then maybe generic investor
sentiment.
I want to focus sort of on the first two as being fundamental drivers of risk.
I'm curious as to your thoughts, how much of market risk do you think comes from changes
in discount rates versus how much a market risk comes from changes in earnings expectations,
and how does this influence your choice of using cyclically adjusted earnings yield and long-term
momentum as your primary variables?
This idea that the equity market is more volatile than you would get from just changes in earnings
expectations or earnings realizations, this goes back to the seminal paper by Bob Schiller,
that's probably one of the top papers of his and contributions that led to his Nobel
prize.
What Schiller did in this paper is he said, let's just take a look at the last 100 years
of U.S. corporate earnings, and let's just go decade by decade, so it's not a lot
of data, we'll go decade by decade, and we'll see how much did earnings change from decade
to decade, and what he found was that when it's annualized in the relevant way, averaging
some of them together, that earnings volatility was way, way lower than would be consistent
with the stock market volatility that we've witnessed historically.
Many, many other academics and practitioners have focused their attention on this, and
they all come to the same place, so John Campbell, professor at Harvard and collaborator and
